confidence_note: Study guides only. Law of the Sea (U.S.-India, MIT model) and cut-and-choose come from one detailed guide; wording kept general. The car-haggling scene and insurance-claim figures from the old/guide text were dropped as unverified.
facts: The authors urge negotiators to insist on objective criteria: fair standards independent of either side's will.
Examples of standards: market value, replacement cost, precedent, scientific judgment, professional standards, efficiency, reciprocity.
The principle is stated as: yield to principle, not to pressure.
At the Law of the Sea Conference, the U.S. and India disagreed on whether mining companies should pay a fee to start mining.
After looking at an economic model developed at MIT, both reconsidered and neither had to back down.
For dividing a dessert, 'one cuts, the other chooses' gives the cutter a reason to cut evenly.
A reciprocity test: would the other side accept the same terms if positions were reversed?
scene_details: one person cutting, the other choosing
tension: Two sides can each give in without either losing face if they both defer to a standard neither of them owns.
opening_idea: Open on the dessert knife: one person cuts, the other chooses.

lessons.idea: A standard outside both parties lets each side agree without feeling beaten by the other.
lessons.anchor: The MIT model that moved the U.S. and India.

reflect_final: In a price or shared-cost conversation, which outside figure or fair rule could both of you accept before anyone names a number?

use_cases.situation: Splitting a shared bill or chore list
use_cases.move: Like cut-and-choose, let one person divide and the other pick first.
Ask which market comparison the price rests on and share yours.

use_cases.situation: A friend asks to borrow money again
use_cases.move: Ask what you would both call fair if roles were reversed.

pocket_idea: Divide by a rule neither of you owns, like one cuts and the other chooses.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: At the Law of the Sea talks, an MIT model let both sides change course without either backing down.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Fisher and Ury say to yield to principle, not pressure. When the U.S. and India disagreed on a mining fee, an MIT economic model gave both a reason to reconsider. Dividing a dessert works the same way: one cuts, the other chooses.
